newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Indonesian cocoa quality must improve - Rabobank.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian cocoa quality must improve - Rabobank.

text.p: Indonesia is the third largest cocoa grower in the world but its image on international markets as a poor quality producer must change if export growth is to be sustained, Dutch agri-bank Rabobank said in a report.
The report noted that of all the major producers, Indonesia had the best prospect to raise output as low production costs (labour and land) combined with access to technology.
The government has said it wanted to achieve a 2.8 percent per annum increase in acreage during the five-year plan (1993-1998) and a 10 percent increase in annual production.
The government's transmigration policy has had a great impact in this area, where cocoa production has been stimulated in the east of the country (Sulawesi).
These more isolated regions with poor infrastructure, sparse population and ample land make them especially fit for cocoa production, the report said.

Higher yields are also being achieved. Rabobank said smallholders are being encouraged by the government to use higher yield seedlings which produce cocoa with a higher fat content and pods with thinner shells.
But more has to be done to combat the crop's poor image.

"Although Indonesian cooca beans are classified as high in solid fat content, the international market regards them as low quality because of the imperfection of the fermentation process and because of the taste, which differs from that preferred in the main consuming countries," the report said.
One of the main problems is with the fermentation process, where smallholders sell their beans as quickly as possible before fermentation has finished.
Another problem is with pod borer, a disease which currently affects around 40,000 acres and is the main reason behind current acreage of 280,000 hectares falling short of the targeted 325,000.
But if these problems can be tackled, Rabobank said the prospects for the Indonesian cocoa sector are good, particularly as local demand is expected to grow sharply.
"If efforts to improve the quality of both beans and processing continue, Indonesia has enormous potential as a producer for the region," it said.
